The words

Lord of mercy, at Thy gate,
Needy souls imploring pray;
Have we come, Good Lord, too late?
Must we turn in grief away?

Young and old Thy mercy claim, —
Some are early at the gate,
Some are late to own Thy name,
Surely none, though late, too late!

Blessed, who with morning sun,
Hopeful at Thy portals wait;
Yea, and when the day is done,
Blessed they who find the gate.

Ah, Good Lord, when Thou wert here,
Homeless, in our world of sin,
Few, to give Thee warmth and cheer,
Called their weary Lord within.

Sad, repenting, full of fear,
Hoping, doubting, still we wait;
As we call, in mercy hear; —
Open, Lord, to us the gate.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum G and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on m (B).
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

John Brownlie translated these words from the Greek service books for Hymns from the Morningland (Paisley, 1911).

The book printed the words without tunes. They are in Sevens (7.7.7.7), and this page sets them to VIENNA; any other Sevens tune fits them as well.

  • Words: Traditional Greek
  • Translated (1911): John Brownlie (1857–1925)
  • Music (1799): Justin Heinrich Knecht (died undefined)

Questions about Lord of Mercy, at Thy Gate

What is the doh of Lord of Mercy, at Thy Gate?

In this version, in G major, doh is G. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Lord of Mercy, at Thy Gate start on?

It starts on m (B in G major). Find doh first, then sing up or down to m.

Is Lord of Mercy, at Thy Gate in the public domain?

Yes. John Brownlie died in 1925, Justin Heinrich Knecht died in undefined; the words were in print by 1911 and the music in 1799. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
